X_EFW_E02_S01_VIS.text: Present-day framing should be brief and quiet. Theo and Rae sit with Adrian in an old archive room, each describing the Desert Marker memory without trying to perform certainty. Theo remembers Starbreaker's fear of waiting. Rae remembers people being moved out before the catastrophe. They cannot reconcile the perspectives. Adrian tells them both happened. A phrase from the old argument—something each remembers in a different voice—pulls the issue into the past. Once the memory begins, leave the present behind for most of the issue.

X_EFW_E02_S02_VIS.text: Ancient Desert Marker, before the battle tips into catastrophe. Treat the setting as lived-in wartime space, not an effects showcase. Starbreaker and Mero have clearly had versions of this conversation before. Starbreaker is tired, not theatrical. Mero's authority comes from listening longer than everyone wants him to. Do not show ancient Theo. Do not explain any weapon or field. The immediate question is whether waiting leaves more people alive or gives the threat time to widen.

X_EFW_E02_S03_VIS.text: Redlin enters as the issue's new champion. Avoid a grand entrance. He comes in dusty, carrying evidence of having been among ordinary people, irritated that Starbreaker has once again been arguing in his absence. His first scene should establish old familiarity: he knows exactly which sentence Starbreaker will use; Starbreaker knows exactly what Redlin will object to. Let the barbs imply years of respect and disappointment. Redlin's philosophy is visible through what he protects, not through technical language about containment.

X_EFW_E02_S04_VIS.text: Redlin takes Mero into a civilian shelter because he refuses to let the decision remain abstract. Children, exhausted workers, an old person who refuses to leave a box of household objects—small human details matter. Redlin knows names. Mero is not unmoved; the scene hurts because he already understands the cost and still has to decide. No casualty projections. No percentages. The political argument becomes: does knowing the people you may sacrifice change whether sacrifice is permissible?

X_EFW_E02_S05_VIS.text: Starbreaker gets his own humanizing scene. He brings Mero to a ridge overlooking evidence of earlier places lost because action came too late. Do not turn the view into a tactical map. Show ruined settlements, evacuation fires, abandoned belongings. Starbreaker has carried too many endings he believes could have been prevented. He is frightening because his argument is emotionally understandable. Mero sees why people follow him. Starbreaker should not be smug; he thinks he is asking to bear responsibility others keep postponing.

X_EFW_E02_S06_VIS.text: Back in the war room, Mero attempts a pause. Starbreaker and Redlin reveal the circularity of their relationship: each believes the other's signature virtue has become a vice. Their argument should feel like an old friendship or alliance that has been worn raw by repeated crises. Mero's question about whether they remember speaking without a battlefield should land as personal loss, not rhetorical wisdom.

X_EFW_E02_S07_VIS.text: Follow Redlin outside. No diagrams, barriers or field terminology. He is physically present with evacuees, moving people through danger, taking weight from an injured stranger, giving simple instructions. This is the reader's clearest experience of why people trust him. His containment principle is embodied as: keep the disaster from reaching the next person. The sequence should be almost entirely human-scale.

X_EFW_E02_S08_VIS.text: Starbreaker and Redlin meet alone on the ridge. Strip away factional audience and command posture. For a moment they are two people who remember each other before the war hardened them. Each asks the other to stop. Neither can because each believes stopping would betray everyone already lost. This scene should seed the possibility of a deeper personal history without locking a specific betrayal that earlier development left unresolved.

X_EFW_E02_S09_VIS.text: The crisis finally crosses the point where every choice is catastrophic. Do not describe mechanics. The sky begins behaving impossibly; distant structures fold into light; people below realize something is wrong before anyone can name it. Mero calls Starbreaker's name once. Starbreaker acts. Redlin does not stand aside—he keeps trying to protect what can still be protected. The moment should feel like two incompatible forms of courage colliding, not one hero defeating another.

X_EFW_E02_S10_VIS.text: Aftermath: glass dust falls through violet light. Let silence dominate. Starbreaker says the threat stopped. Redlin looks at the dead and displaced. Both statements are true. Mero refuses the comfort of choosing one truth over the other. This is the first time the reader should understand the war's deeper trap: each side can point to real lives saved by its logic and real lives destroyed by the other side's failure.

X_EFW_E02_S11_VIS.text: Return abruptly to the present. Theo and Rae are both shaken, but by different parts of the memory. They compare small human details rather than lore: Theo remembers fear in Starbreaker's face; Rae remembers Redlin carrying a child. Each detail was absent from the other's experience. Do not show ancient Theo or Rae. Their absence from the memory remains invisible as a clue rather than an obvious omission.

X_EFW_E02_S12_VIS.text: Outside under ordinary rain, Theo asks the dangerous question: how can two living people remember private details from the same forgotten day from different places? Adrian's answer deliberately avoids identity. Rae notices. Theo asks directly whether either of them was there. Adrian says, 'Not tonight.' Do not play it as cute cryptic dialogue; Adrian is choosing to postpone a truth he believes they are not ready to survive. End on Rae recognizing that his refusal is not the same as denial.
